newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's centrists present pro-European platform.
newsitem.headline: France's centrists present pro-European platform.

text.p: The junior partner in France's ruling coalition on Wednesday presented a strongly pro-European platform for next month's snap election, stressing that France must join the single European currency in 1999.

The head of the centrist Union for French Democracy (UDF), Francois Leotard, said the platform reflected that of its senior partner, the Rally for the Republic (RPR), by insisting on cutting taxes and public spending and rolling back the state.

He told a news conference the only differences were on the extent of decentralisation, saying UDF wanted to push further than the Gaullist RPR of President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

Conservative Juppe presented on Tuesday a programme for the May 25-June 1 election stressing continuation of current policies rather than radical change, while seeking to unite his centre-right coalition behind him.
Leotard said the two partners would publish a joint platform early next week and iron out on Thursday the last remaining differences on fielding joint candidates in most constituencies.

He said any UDF dissident resisting his order to stand down for a Gaullist candidate would be sacked from the party within minutes. "I will be merciless as the battle ahead will be tough and brief and cannot be won without discipline," Leotard, an ex-defence minister, said.
UDF had 206 seats to the Rally for the Republic's 258 in the outgoing assembly. Opinion polls generally see the ruling coalition retaining power with a reduced majority.
UDF's programme said the euro was indispensable to create monetary stability that would attract investment to Europe and favour economic growth and employment.
"This is the reason why achieving the single currency on January 1, 1999 is a non-negotiable objective for UDF," it said.
He attacked the opposition Socialists, who have indicated they may try to soften the Maastricht Treaty three per cent budget deficit criterion for joining the euro.

"The Socialists have largely dropped their European ideals as the price for getting Communist votes," he said. The Socialists ae seeking an electoral alliance with the Communists, who have demanded a referendum on the single currency.

Pleading for the European Union to become more democratic in order to appeal to the ordinary citizen, it advocated boosting the European Parliament's control over the European Commission, and associating national parliaments to the Commission's work.
The platform proposed to cut the role of the state, continue privatisations and pass a plan to cut public spending by five percent over five years.
In order to boost economic growth and employment, it proposed to cut labour costs and abolish payroll taxes, both for employers and wage-earners, on the first 1,500 francs ($280) of salaries.
Leotard pledged to refuse to vote in the next parliament any measure that would increase taxes or payroll levies.

The UDF also suggested cutting the presidential term from seven to five years to make it coincide with the parliamentary term, a poposal that has been made before but was ignored by serving presidents.
